item.title: Investors await CBA correction to kickstart mining resurgence
item.description:
A major rotation in Australia’s sharemarket is expected this financial year as investors finally cash in on the dazzling rally in bank stocks led by Commonwealth Bank to chase a long-awaited resurgence in the beaten-down mining sector.

Bank stocks soared 26 per cent in the 12 months through June, fuelled by an astonishing 45 per cent rally in CBA as superannuation giants, passive funds and offshore managers piled into Australia’s largest lender.

The sheer momentum of FY25’s hottest trade sucked capital away from the S&P/ASX 200’s other major sector, resources, which dropped 8 per cent as the mining behemoths were hit by ongoing weakness in China’s property market and the iron ore price.

But brokers are warning that any rotation between banks and the mining sector would likely be swift and painful for those caught off guard.

While most analysts agree that CBA’s valuation is exorbitant, a key question for the market is what will be the catalyst to get investors to sell? MST Marquee’s Hasan Tevfik suggests “common sense [could] prevail”, which would stop investors buying what is now the world’s most expensive bank.

“There’s been situations in the past where there’s been this unusual re-rating – you don’t need the money to move out of CBA and into BHP, for example, you just need inflows into CBA to stop,” MST’s senior investment strategist told The Australian Financial Review.

“At that point, the stock would de-rate as super funds accept they don’t need an equal weight position of 12 per cent in CBA and just settle for an 8 per cent or 10 per cent allocation, which then forces them to buy other stocks.”

CBA’s share of the S&P/ASX 200 has ballooned over the past 12 months from 9 per cent to just shy of 12 per cent. It has meant that those fund managers who avoided buying the stock, or held a smaller weighting than the benchmark index, typically underperformed over that period.

As a result, portfolio managers are this year facing significant pressure to get their allocation to resources and banks right, given the two sectors make up almost half of the ASX.

Tevfik has held a net short position in the banks since September last year and believes the major miners are not being valued correctly by the market – a dynamic which he expects to reverse in the next 12 months.

“There’s going to be something that changes in investors’ minds – these are high-quality companies,” he said.

Investment bank Citi is among those warning of a sudden rotation in the ASX.

Traders got a taste of this in September last year, when hopes for Chinese stimulus saw BHP outperform CBA by 20 per cent in just five days. When Beijing failed to meet expectations, the outperformance gradually unwound over a month.

Cautionary tale

“It stands as a cautionary tale as to the potential swiftness of a rotation when the market receives its ‘catalyst’, particularly when CBA and BHP collectively make up 20 per cent of the ASX 200,” said Citi’s head of Australian banks research, Tom Strong.

While investors in the resource sector are betting on a reallocation of capital away from bank stocks, they are also not expecting the money to flow straight into the big iron ore miners as it has done in the past.

Perennial portfolio manager Sam Berridge said that’s because of a shift in Beijing’s stimulus away from steel-intensive sectors that are reliant on iron ore and towards manufacturing and domestic consumption.

While Berridge is positioning for a broad rally in raw material prices over the next year, he is betting it will be fuelled by commodities used in the manufacturing process like aluminium, copper and rare earths.

“If we get a normalisation of this trade war and the US continues to cut rates because tariffs aren’t as inflationary as expected, that should sow the seeds for a decent commodities rally towards the end of this calendar year and certainly into 2026,” he said.

Perennial’s Strategic Natural Resources Fund is avoiding the major iron ore miners and is instead betting on copper stocks such as Hudbay Minerals and Firefly Metals, gold companies Ramelius Resources and Turaco Gold and rare earths miners including Brazilian Rare Earths.
item.author: Alex Gluyas

item.title: 13 big calls these ASX giants must nail in the new financial year
item.description:
Australia’s biggest companies will spend the first weeks of the new financial year frantically closing off their books, completing their audits and deciding which version of underlying earnings will most impress their investors ahead of the August reporting season.

But after that annual rush several blue-chip ASX firms will get back down to the serious business of mulling strategic calls that could shape their next decade as a listed company.

Do we buy? Do we sell? Where does our leg of growth come from? Who is the best person to lead us to the promised land?

Boards are always dealing with such questions. But with the ASX trading near record levels, and the external environment as uncertain as it’s been for many years, the pressure to make the right calls has arguably never been greater.

Here are 13 potentially make-or-break moments that our biggest companies are facing in 2025-26.

Can Santos win over Jim Chalmers?

Santos’ deal to sell itself to Abu Dhabi Inc will come down to whether the South Australian giant and its suitor XRG can win Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ rubber stamp.

XRG has made promises to keep Santos in South Australia, but Chalmers may need firm guarantees around the level of investment the Emirati giant is willing to make to boost Australian gas supplies over the coming decade.

Does Woolworths sell or kill Big W?

Last week, Woolworths chief executive Amanda Bardwell shuttered online marketplace MyDeal, but in the coming months, she’ll need to decide the future of discount department store chain Big W and the group’s struggling New Zealand food business.

Neither moves the dial at Woolworths, where every ounce of attention needs to be put into the flagship Australian supermarkets division. But both are large businesses and large employers, which makes these emotive decisions.

Who is Rio Tinto’s next CEO?

The sudden departure of Rio boss Jakob Stausholm in May, raises two questions: who gets the top job, and what riding instructions will they be given by chairman Dominic Barton?

Current iron ore boss Simon Trott looks the most likely candidate, but how aggressively Barton wants to chase growth is the bigger question.

Rio’s Simandou iron ore mine will be completed this financial year, while investors will want proof Stausholm’s big bet on lithium is paying off. But does Rio need another deal to set up its next two decades?

When does Commonwealth Bank CEO Matt Comyn call time?

Australia’s most respected chief executive is in his seventh year in charge, meaning succession issues are likely to be on the mind of the CBA board and Comyn himself.

CBA’s surging share price had grabbed global attention, and the value of Comyn’s personal stock is such that big offshore companies could offer him a job.

The end of the Comyn era at CBA will be a real moment, and one to be handled carefully.

How does REA Group fight off CoStar?

REA Group is also hunting for a new chief executive after Owen Wilson announced his retirement in February.

The next boss had better be ready for action. First, there’s the little matter of a probe by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission to deal with.

But then there’s the question of how to fight off US giant CoStar, which has acquired REA’s great rival Domain from Nine Entertainment (publisher of this masthead) for $2.8 billion.

History says CoStar’s approach is to try and undercut the market leader, crimping industry profitability to win market share. Figuring out a plan of defence will be the first task for Wilson’s successor.

How does Nine Entertainment spend the Domain proceeds?

This is the other side of the CoStar deal. Investors will get a big capital return, but how much Nine chief executive Matt Stanton retains to fund his growth plans, and whether he has investor backing for deals, will be closely watched.

Will ASX need to blow itself up to save itself?

ASIC chairman Joe Longo wants the watchdog’s probe into market operator ASX Limited to have the same sort of impact that the prudential probe into CBA had back in 2017.

That suggests ASX boss Helen Lofthouse and David Clarke are going to face big pressure to deliver big change to the organisation. Will that be limited to culture, governance and accountability, or will it require more structural simplification, as we saw at CBA?

Does ANZ keep or kill ANZ Plus?

New ANZ boss Nuno Matos has made no secret of his desire to go faster on ANZ’s new retail banking tech platform, ANZ Plus.

While the need for ANZ to update its technology stack is undeniable, how radically Matos wants to reshape the Plus project will depend on the results of a review he has underway.

Matos is said to have shaken up ANZ’s culture already; abandoning ANZ Plus would certainly send a signal.

Does Perpetual have a plan C, D and E?

In February, the ATO effectively killed any chance private equity giant KKR would be able to complete its takeover of Perpetual.

Four months on, the company’s future isn’t any more settled.

Perpetual’s wealth management business is up for sale, with a price of between $500 million and $700 million and plenty of private equity interest.

But with the stock still 25 per cent below its recent peak in February, it seems investors want a more concrete turnaround plan from chief executive Bernard Reilly.

Does Origin keep Octopus Energy?

The stunning success of Origin Energy’s punt on British energy retailer Octopus Energy and its software platform Kraken has created a fascinating conundrum for the architect of the deal, chief executive Frank Calabria: how and when does he crystallise value for Origin shareholders?

Origin’s stake is in the books for $1.26 billion, but would be worth many multiples of that, and even more if the Kraken business – which is where the value is – gets spun out eventually. It’s a quality problem to have.

Will Treasury Wine Estate need to go even further upmarket?

Sam Fischer, the next chief executive of Treasury Wine Estates, will start on September 30 with a decent hangover: the stock is down 30 per cent this year, as investors fret about a global wine glut and pressures on its American and Chinese business.

Fischer will arrive in the midst of TWE’s restructuring into three divisions: the Penfolds and Treasury Americas luxury units and the Treasury Collective premium wine unit.

The latter, where wine sells for 80 per cent less than the luxury divisions, looks distinctly out of place.

Can Dexus regain investor trust after Melbourne Airport stoush?

It’s the legal fight the business community is salivating over: Dexus versus several of its fellow shareholders in Australia Pacific Airports Corporation, which owns Melbourne and Launceston Airports.

Investors, including IFM and the Future Fund, have claimed Dexus inappropriately used confidential information to attract new investors.

Dexus denies and is fighting the claims, but how this fight plays out will determine how hard chief executive Ross Du Vernet will need to work to win back the trust of some of the country’s biggest investors.

Who follows King Richard at WiseTech Global?

As the executive chairman of WiseTech Global, Richard White has a bit on his plate just now: running the company, overseeing its corporate governance rebuild and executing on the $3.2 billion acquisition of e2open.

But the question of who gets the job as chief executive of the company is another task on the to-do list.

White will clearly lead the appointment and remain in control of WiseTech’s future strategy, but investors will want to be sure White isn’t picking a yes-person.

item.title: ASX rises; SGH drops after Boral boss steps down
item.description:
ASX rises; SGH drops after Boral boss steps down

Australian shares edged higher on the back of tech stocks and the supermarkets after New York shook off some mid-session nerves with both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite resetting the closing record highs.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 24.3 points, 0.3 per cent, to 8566.6 in the opening five minutes of trading on Tuesday, with nine out of the 11 sectors in the green.

SGH dropped 4.9 per cent following news that Vik Bansal will step down as chief executive of Boral and transition to a role as non-executive director of SGH.

Insignia Financial jumped 9.4 per cent CC Capital said it continues to “actively work towards making a binding bid for the company” and would finalise financing and investment committee approvals in the next two weeks.

The biggest US banks were higher after passing the Federal Reserve’s annual stress test, setting the stage for payouts. Hewlett Packard Enterprise rose 11 per cent, the most in the S&P 500, after the US Department of Justice settled its lawsuit challenging the firm’s takeover of Juniper Networks.

Oracle reset its record high on a cloud-services deal worth $US30 billion ($45 billion) a year.

In a note, market strategy firm Yardeni Research said so far, the current bull market looks like a normal one, with the potential to match the returns of some of the best bull markets since the mid-1960s.

“We are still targeting 6500 on the S&P 500 stock price index by the end of this year and 10,000 by the end of the ‘Roaring 2020s’ decade. It’s a bit hard to believe, but the main risk at this time may be a stock market melt-up, i.e. a speculative bubble. That’s where we were only four and a half months ago when the latest correction started.”

Investors await CBA correction to kickstart mining resurgence

A major rotation in Australia’s sharemarket is expected this financial year as investors finally cash in on the dazzling rally in bank stocks led by Commonwealth Bank to chase a long-awaited resurgence in the beaten-down mining sector.

Bank stocks soared 26 per cent in the 12 months through June, fuelled by an astonishing 45 per cent rally in CBA as superannuation giants, passive funds and offshore managers piled into Australia’s largest lender.

The sheer momentum of FY25’s hottest trade sucked capital away from the S&P/ASX 200’s other major sector, resources, which dropped 8 per cent as the mining behemoths were hit by ongoing weakness in China’s property market and the iron ore price.

IAG reports insurance profit guidance increase

Insurance giant IAG has reported insurance profit guidance has increased to $1.6 billion to $1.8 billion, up from $1.4 billion to $1.6 billion.

IAG’s reported insurance margin guidance range has also increased “toward the top end” of 15.5 per cent to 17.5 per cent, up from 13.5 per cent to 15.5 per cent.

TPG Telecom director Serpil Timuray resigns

TPG Telecom has announced that Serpil Timuray resigned as a director of the company on Monday. TPG will announce when the appointment of another director to fill the casual vacancy occurs.

Vik Bansal to step down as Boral CEO

Vik Bansal will step down as chief executive of Boral and transition to a role as non-executive director of SGH (Seven Group Holdings).

The transition is expected to occur early next year.

“SGH has worked closely with Mr Bansal on a structured succession to ensure a smooth leadership transition and the continued execution of Boral’s performance journey,” SGH said in a statement.

Matt McKenzie, currently executive general manager of concrete and quarries, has also been appointed chief operating officer, effective today.

SGH acquired Boral in July last year.

Downer sells 49pc stake in Kelois Downer joint venture

Downer EDI has announced it will sell its 49 per cent stake in the Keolis Downer joint venture to Keolis Group.

The sale price implies an enterprise value of $132 million, with Downer to receive cash proceeds for its 49 per cent share at the completion of the transaction.

Separately, Downer also announced it has been awarded a three-year extension to its gas services contract with AusNet, valued at about $200 million.

Commencing in April, and following the completion of the current contract term, the contract extension will see Downer continue to provide operations, maintenance, asset replacement, capital works and meter reading services across AusNet’s entire gas distribution network.

CC Capital ‘actively’ working towards bid for Insignia Financial

CC Capital has informed Insignia Financial that it continues to actively work towards making a binding bid for the company.

CC Capital is finalising financing and investment committee approvals, a process that is expected to be completed in the next two weeks, Insignia said.

“There is no certainty that the ongoing discussions will result in any transaction being put to Insignia Financial shareholders for their consideration,” the company said.

“Insignia Financial will continue to keep the market informed in accordance with its continuous disclosure obligations.”

Talga appoints former Swedish employment minister to board

Perth-based battery materials company Talga has announced Eva Nordmark will join its board as a non-executive director from July 14.

Nordmark, a former Swedish employment and gender equality minister, has served as chair of Talga’s Swedish subsidiary, Talga AB, since December 2023.

The company also announced the retirement of non-executive directors Stephen Lowe and Ola Rinnan as of June 30.

Serko renews technology partnership with Flight Centre

Serko has renewed its technology partnership with Flight Centre, which it said accounts for a “significant proportion” of its booking volume across Australia and New Zealand.

“Flight Centre has been a key contributor to Serko’s success, and this renewal lays the foundation for us to continue to expand our relationship and co-develop unique capabilities for Flight Centre customers on our platform,” said Serko chief executive Darrin Grafton.

Trump floats Japan tariff, Hassett says deals after July 4

US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose a fresh tariff level on Japan, while his top economic adviser says the White House aims to finalise deals with partners after the July 4 holiday.

Trump’s latest round of brinkmanship with Tokyo on Monday (Tuesday AEST) comes just over a week before a July 9 deadline for higher tariffs to restart for dozens of trading partners, including Japan.

He cited what he said was the country’s unwillingness to accept US rice exports.

“They won’t take our RICE, and yet they have a massive rice shortage,” Trump posted on social media. “In other words, we’ll just be sending them a letter, and we love having them as a Trading Partner for many years to come.”

Meanwhile, White House National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett signalled that agreements with several governments would be announced after US Independence Day. He said the administration’s focus has been on passing Trump’s massive tax and spending bill through Congress before the holiday.

“It might be that people take an hour or two off on the Fourth to watch the fireworks and then we’ll get back, and we’re going to start to announce the frameworks,” Hassett told Fox on Monday. “We’re expecting to meet with the president and explain the frameworks that have been negotiated and see if he approves or not.”

Struggling semiconductor firm Wolfspeed files for bankruptcy

Wolfspeed, a chipmaker caught in President Donald Trump’s push to reshape Biden-era tech subsidies, filed for bankruptcy to enact a creditor-backed plan to slash $US4.6 billion ($6.9 billion) in debt.

The North Carolina-based company filed petitions for reorganisation under Chapter 11, according to a statement released on Monday (Tuesday AEST). It expects to emerge from bankruptcy by the end of the third quarter, it said.

The filing marks one of the largest bankruptcies so far this year, behind only Brazilian airline Azul SA and satellite company Ligado Networks, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
item.author: Gus McCubbing, Timothy Moore

item.title: The ASX’s bumper year makes for bullish investors (despite the chaos)
item.description:
The Australian sharemarket has recorded its best financial year since the pandemic as investors shrugged off the Trump administration’s chaotic trade policies and instability in the Middle East to push local stocks up more than 10 per cent and towards record highs.

Powered largely by big gains in Commonwealth Bank, Westpac and Wesfarmers, the S&P/ASX 200 Index had its best year since 2021, when investors piled back into the market after the COVID-19 slump.

CBA, the country’s largest bank and most valuable company, was responsible for 47 per cent of the index’s gain over the 12 months alone.

And major investors are optimistic for the next year, despite a seeming disconnect between share prices and earnings expectations at some of the biggest companies.

Ten Cap portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu predicted the market would keep rising for six months as the Reserve Bank of Australia cuts interest rates, buoying spending and profits.

“Any point in time when the RBA cuts rates, and we’re not in a recession, is a very bullish sign for equity markets, particularly in a market where a lot of the uncertainties, like trade, are already well known,” Liu said.

“Soon you will see people deploy capital in a big way into the market.

“I’m pretty optimistic. I think the market will continue to climb, and for many that are not fully invested, they’ll be forced back in.”

The ASX 200 rose 28.1 points or 0.3 per cent on Monday, the final trading day of the financial year, to end at 8542.3.

Investors, optimistic that US President Donald Trump would sign deals averting the return to short-lived tariffs announced in April, had pushed Wall Street to record highs last week.

The bullishness of the market is at odds with the tumult of the past six months, volatility that only increased after Trump took office.

Investors have cycled through all manner of strategies, from the Trump trade, which suggested any investment in the US would be profitable, to the TACO trade, which implied the president would always back down.

Now, the market is mulling the momentum trade, a bet on whatever happens to be going up.

And plenty of stocks are going up, with the so-called “magnificent seven” technology companies recovering after a steep fall in April, and consumer confidence lifting as the White House slowly walks away from the worst of the tariffs threatened during “liberation day”.

The ASX 200 has jumped more than 16 per cent since its April low, when $97 billion was carved from the market on one day over fears that prolonged tariff uncertainty would put the brakes on earnings and spending.

The enormous falls in sharemarkets, including Wall Street, left some of the world’s most prominent investors, such as American billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman, pleading with Trump to stop the trade turmoil. Ackman described it as “an economic nuclear war”.

Trump pushed the biggest tariffs into July, and has been negotiating ever since.

That has left the ASX 200 up 10 per cent in the 12 months to June 30, after a 7.8 per cent rise last financial year. It rose 9.6 per cent in the year to the end of June 2023, and fell 7.5 per cent in the preceding 12 months.

Still, not every investor is convinced the market will keep rising.

“While Australia has levers to weather current volatility in a relative sense, meaningful index upside seems capped for now given where valuation multiples sit,” Morgan Stanley Wealth Management’s Alex Ventelon said.

SPI Asset Management partner Stephen Innes said: “This rally’s been running on liquidity pipe dreams. With every macro print and fiscal headline acting like a speed bump or a slingshot, expect a volatile July.

“Wall Street’s fireworks show came a bit early this year, with the S&P and Nasdaq blowing through record highs like a bottle rocket strapped to a jetpack.”

Innes pointed to the next minefields for the market: fears unemployment will rise, a deteriorating US budget, and the Federal Reserve’s “ever-wobbly independence” as Trump attacks the central bank’s chairman, Jerome Powell, calling for him to lower interest rates quickly or resign.

On Monday, Trump floated the idea of keeping higher tariffs on some imports, signalling the trade uncertainties were far from over.

“So we give Japan no cars. They won’t take our cars, right? And yet we take millions and millions of their cars into the US. It’s not fair,” he said in an interview. “They could take a lot of oil. They could take a lot of other things.”

Those problems are in the future. For the country’s big superannuation funds, a good result – returns are already set for the year.

SuperRatings executive director Kirby Rappell said the past 12 months had been a “really strong financial year for super funds, with returns above the long-term average” of about 7 per cent.

“It looks like, for some of the top-performing funds, returns this year will be in the double-digits,” he added.

Cbus and MLC are already projecting their high-growth funds to record returns of between 10 per cent and 11 per cent for the financial year.

The average balanced superannuation option was likely to return a 10.2 per cent return over the financial year, according to analysts at Chant West, a research and data firm that specialises in wealth management.

“The year really highlights the importance of thinking long term and being patient,” said Chant West investment research manager Mano Mohankumar.

“Some members may have been tempted to move to cash or conservative options due to market volatility, but the problem when you switch is you lock in the losses and miss out on the subsequent rebound.”

Equities were not the only market rising this year. Cryptocurrencies have been on a wild ride, surging when Trump was inaugurated, given his strong support for digital currencies and the fever around the $TRUMP meme coin.

Having reached a market capitalisation of $US9 billion ($13.8 billion), the $TRUMP coin has slid to just $US1.79 billion over the year.

Bitcoin, on the other hand, has jumped more than 77 per cent in that time.

Gold is up almost a quarter this year, and is trading around $US230 short of a record high in April, when investors sought a refuge from the turmoil caused by the Trump administration’s trade policies.

It has been falling over the past two weeks, however, reflecting the market’s mood to take more risks.

The speed of the sentiment shift since April will keep big investors guessing well into the new financial year.

“We were surprised by the speed at which both the market and investor sentiment has rebounded post the 90-day delay in the Trump administration’s tariff implementation,” said Stephen Butel, a portfolio manager at Platypus Asset Management.
item.author: Joanne Tran, Lucas Baird

item.title: Tetratherix jumps on debut, capping strong week of ASX listings
item.description:
Tetratherix has become the sixth company to successfully list on the ASX in the past week, with shares in the tissue and bone repair treatment manufacturer jumping more than 7 per cent on their debut.

Five of those companies – including Virgin Australia and Greatland Resources, a gold producer backed by the billionaire Forrest family – remain above their IPO prices as investors flock to newly listed stocks.

“In terms of leading indicators for the Australian market, the number of recent IPOs has been an encouraging signal indicating that risk capital is returning to the local equities market since [the COVID-19 pandemic],” said Stephen Butel, a portfolio manager at Platypus Asset Management.

The successful debut of Virgin, which floated at $2.90 a share last Tuesday and is now trading at $3.09, in particular has created a wave of optimism that a years-long dearth of new listings has finally ended.

Tetratherix shares were priced at $2.88, with the company raising about $25 million. They rose to $3.19 during the first day of trade, and closed at $3.02, up 7 per cent. That left the company capitalised at $152 million.

Tetratherix is backed by Radar Ventures, the venture capital fund run by Xero founder Rod Drury. The company produces a treatment called Tetramatrix, a water-based solution that can be injected into wounds and turns into an adhesive hydrogel to help repair tissue and bones.

Tetratherix was founded by University of Sydney biomolecular engineer Ali Fathi, who owns a 28 per cent stake. Fathi, now Tetratherix’s chief technology officer, began developing the product in 2011 as part of his PhD. Will Knox is the chief executive. Knox owns 6.7 per cent of the company and has a background in the industry, having founded and sold his own surgical and implant company uHealth to Device Technologies in 2017.

The company, in its prospectus, told investors it would use the money raised with the ASX listing to expand a manufacturing site and to fund more research and development of products derived from Tetramatrix. “Following successful proof of concept pilot human studies for specific clinical indications, the company’s business model focuses on licensing its intellectual property to targeted market leaders,” the prospectus said.

Argo Investments emerged as one of the Tetratherix’s largest investors on Monday. Argo analyst Paul Frost said the company had “an interesting business model in the context of the partnerships they’ve established, the commercial arrangements and the co-development arrangements that they’ve embedded within these master agreements”.

Frost said that because Tetratherix’s product was considered a medical device its path through regulatory approvals would be “shorter”.

Tetratherix is the 13th listing on the ASX this year. The last big year for floats was in 2021, when more than 180 companies hit the bourse, some of which had been partly delayed by the pandemic.

“You’ve got substantial private equity and private credit market capital floating around that needs to be deployed,” Frost said.

“[For companies] it’s a choice between the costs of an IPO against remaining in private hands.”

Australian Eagle Asset Management portfolio manager Alan Kwan also said the number of recent IPOs was a “positive” signal for the local market.

“Last week, we had another listing with Greatland, the gold economy. And Virgin last week has been encouraging, given that the few years have been characterised by a lack of private equity exits,” Kwan said.
item.author: Luke Kinsella

item.title: A new bubble may be forming. But investors will love it
item.description:
The new financial year is about to start in a way that seemed unthinkable just a few short months ago.

The S&P 500 set a new all-time high on Friday night, dispatching the dark days of early April – when the world economy and financial markets reeled from US President Donald Trump’s tariffs announcement – to the annals of history.

Meanwhile, the ASX 200 sits less than 1 per cent below its record level reached earlier this month, despite the Australian market set to record its third straight year of declining profits.

At this point, your columnist would usually tell you how silly all this feels. About how, in the words of Vantage Point Asset Management chief investment officer Nick Ferres, there is a “divergence between price, beliefs, and fundamentals” whereby investors are not being compensated for these clear and present risks still hanging over the markets – from the highest tariffs in 90 years, the American debt crisis, geopolitics, to the growing evidence of trouble in the US labour market, which Ferres says is showing cracks that look remarkably similar to 2008, before everything fell apart.

“Just like in 2008, we may be mistaking lagging indicators (like the unemployment rate) for structural health, when leading indicators (job cut announcements) are screaming stress,” Ferres says. “Several major questions remain unresolved, and yet the market is behaving as though it is all clear. Moreover, the benign outcome is already well-priced.”

But rightly or wrongly, the bulls are in the ascendancy, and it behoves even the biggest bear to look at the case that the powerful rally of the last few months can actually keep running.

It all comes down to three powerful forces.

The first is fiscal stimulus. Yes, the US government is in the process of reversing its recent pattern of massive spending growth, with numbers from Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett suggesting US government spending will flip from growing by $US650 billion in 2024 to shrinking by $US50 billion in 2025.

But it’s a different story in Europe and indeed across the NATO nations outside the US. German government spending will jump by $US110 billion this year, with NATO nations to spend $US90 billion in 2026. Even China is getting in on the act, with Hartnett estimating that stimulus there will be about $US40 billion.

This helps explain the outperformance of markets outside the US this calendar year. The S&P 500 is up 5 per cent, but non-US stocks are up 15 per cent, with Germany’s equity market up 28 per cent and Hong Kong up 20 per cent.

The second force is rate cuts. Hartnett says this is shaping up to be the biggest year for rate cuts since 2009, when central banks tried to stabilise the economy in the wake of the global financial crisis – 64 so far this year around the globe. As Trump likes to note every five minutes, the Federal Reserve is yet to join the party, but it will in the next six months to support a weakening US economy. The Reserve Bank of Australia has at least a few cuts left in it over the next six months, likely starting in a few weeks.

The third force is Trump. Clearly, he’s been the big swing factor for investors so far this calendar year, and trading his next move has turned out to be far more important than trading market fundamentals.

But Hartnett sees a pivot that creates a real risk of a bubble forming in the second half of the year, as the Fed’s rate cuts and a weaker US dollar combine with a Trump pivot away from tariffs and towards tax cuts, deregulation and growth “as a cure to reduce US debt burden via a boom”.

There are a few assumptions in this prediction, including that the US jobs market doesn’t weaken such that monthly job creation doesn’t fall below 100,000, and that bond yields remain below 5 per cent. Hartnett also concedes that US earnings growth estimates remain ambitious without an unambiguous improvement in global growth readings and AI delivering on its promise by providing a gradual lift in unemployment.

And if that’s not enough, Bank of America’s measures of sentiment suggest that if it’s not time to sell stocks because they’re over-extended, it’s time to take a bit of profit.

“But bubbles ignore trading rules,” Hartnett says, and stocks can keep running even in the face of bearish – or even logical – views on the risk-reward equation in markets, such as presented by Ferres above.

Macquarie’s Viktor Shvets is another who has argued global earnings projections look overdone, but he also says that as the “insanity premium” built into US markets since Trump’s arrival – best seen through the weakness in America – starts to reduce as policy normalises, then the gap between surging European stocks and US stocks could reduce.

Bubbles are dangerous things. Dangerous when they pop, but also dangerous for investors who stay out of them and miss the big gains. Finding the middle ground is extraordinarily difficult.

And if the US market is going to run, investors will need to put their faith in a small group of names.

Hartnett says if the S&P 500 is on the cusp of its seventh big breakout since 1990, it will be a narrow bull market driven by technology stocks. Just 22 S&P 500 stocks are at all-time highs, versus 67 in the rally that started in January 2024, and 54 stocks in the August 2020 surge. Plenty to nourish bulls and bears in that.

item.title: ASX ends FY25 up 10pc, best since 2021
item.description:
ASX rallies on trade talks; CSL, James Hardie climb

The Australian sharemarket climbed on Monday, extending its financial year gain as progress in US trade negotiations boosted investor sentiment.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 28.1 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 8542.3, with seven out of the 11 sectors gaining. Health and technology led the advance.

on Friday and Nvidia towards $US4 trillion ($6.1 trillion) in market capitalisation. Oil and gold were lower amid the increased risk-on environment.

“It’s been a very subdued end of month and end of quarter – usually we expect to see some fireworks at this point, but it hasn’t really delivered,” IG market analyst Tony Sycamore told The Australian Financial Review.

‘Pleasantly surprised’

“But in the context of the rally we’ve seen since April lows, it’s probably a case of portfolio managers being pleasantly surprised by how well the ASX has performed in the run home, and they’re sitting happy, meaning there wasn’t a need to find that extra spark.”

US President Donald Trump told the media over the weekend that he did not think he needed to extend the July 9 tariff deadline for countries negotiating with the US.

Among the countries in talks, India is reported to have extended its stay in Washington to iron out a deal, Canada has withdrawn its digital services tax on technology companies to restart negotiations, and Taiwan has said it made “constructive progress”.

On the ASX, investors have piled into health stocks, with CSL up 2.2 per cent to $239.48, Pro Medicus 1.6 per cent to $285.08, and Sigma Healthcare 1.4 per cent to $2.99.

The tech sector was also well bid, with NextDC finishing up 2.2 per cent to $14.50 while financials edged higher. Macquarie Group climbed 3.9 per cent to $228.73. The big four banks were more mixed with Commonwealth Bank dipping 0.3 per cent to $184.75.

Investors took profits from the big iron ore producers on the last day of the financial year, with Rio Tinto down 1.7 per cent to $107.13, Fortescue down 1.2 per cent to $15.28, and BHP falling 2.1 per cent to $36.75.

Stocks in focus

In corporate news, James Hardie rose 7.1 per cent to $41.70 after shareholders in US outdoor decking company Azek approved a $14 billion buyout, which will see James Hardie shift its primary listing to New York.

Star Entertainment tanked 6.9 per cent to 14¢ after its Hong Kong investors threatened to walk away from a deal for Brisbane’s new Queen’s Wharf casino and hotel complex.

DroneShield fell 4.2 per cent to $2.28 after earlier rallying on news it had won a $9.7 million Latin American defence contract. That’s after last week’s 33 per cent rally from announcing a major European deal.

NIB jumped 9.4 per cent to $7.08 after UBS upgraded the private health insurer to “buy” from “neutral” and set a short-term share price target of $7.85, which implies an upside of more than 20 per cent.

Biotech company Tetratherix jumped 13 per cent in the first few minutes of its debut on the Australian sharemarket, in what is the latest of a handful of initial public offerings this month. It closed at $3.02, up 4.9 per cent.

And Superloop rose 1 per cent to $3.01 after the broadband provider said it expected underlying earnings to reach $91 million for the full year, beating its earlier guidance of $83 million to $88 million.

With Bloomberg

That’s a wrap on today’s news. Join us again soon for .

Bitcoin soars, altcoins fade in $300b crypto shakeout

On the face of it, 2025 looks like a banner year for crypto – bitcoin hitting a record, an industry-boosting US president whose family is venturing headlong into the sector, and key legislation widely expected to be passed by Congress.

But look beyond the bullish headlines and the rally in bitcoin, and a vastly different landscape comes into view. Most of the so-called altcoins once touted as competitors to the original cryptoasset are nursing steep declines, with more than $300 billion of market value wiped out so far this year.

The sea of red points to a wider malaise that’s forcing parts of the industry to confront existential questions.

Crypto was imagined by early enthusiasts as a universe where a host of coins competed for investor money, offering a diverse set of use cases. But as bitcoin reigns supreme, that’s giving way to predictions that large swaths of the sector will become a digital wasteland.

“I think they’re just going to die, frankly,” Nick Philpott, co-founder of trading platform Zodia Markets, said of altcoins. “They’ll just wither away. Technically, a lot of this stuff will just sit there and gather dust in perpetuity.”

Trump says ‘Mr Japan’ unfair on cars, floats keeping 25% tariff

US President Donald Trump floated the idea of keeping 25 per cent tariffs on Japan’s cars as talks between the two nations continued with little more than a week to go before a slew of higher duties are set to kick in if a trade deal isn’t reached.

“So we give Japan no cars. They won’t take our cars, right? And yet we take millions and millions of their cars into the United States. It’s not fair,” Trump said during a Fox News interview that aired on Sunday (Monday AEST).

“Now, we have oil. They could take a lot of oil. They could take a lot of other things,” he said, referring to ways Japan might reduce the US trade deficit.

The comments show that the two sides still remain some distance from an agreement and highlight the risk that Trump may stick with the 25 per cent tariff on cars.

Deal makers hit $1.8 trillion as they get used to trade chaos

Big money takeovers of private companies helped drive mergers and acquisitions in the first half, as deal makers got comfortable writing sizeable checks in topsy-turvy markets.

More than half of the 10 largest deals announced in 2025 have involved a private target, data compiled by Bloomberg shows, including the tie-up of Charter Communications and Cox Communications, Alphabet’s purchase of cybersecurity firm Wiz and Constellation Energy’s acquisition of US power station operator Calpine.

All were valued at around $30 billion or more including debt.

Transactions like these and Meta’s $14 billion-plus investment in data-labelling start-up Scale AI have lifted the value of all deals globally by almost a fifth to $US1.8 trillion, the data shows.

“The creativity we’re seeing across deals is symptomatic of the need to unwind the massive amounts of capital tied up in privately held companies,” said Haidee Lee, global head of sponsor M&A at Goldman Sachs.

ASX rallies on trade talks; CSL, James Hardie climb

The Australian sharemarket climbed, extending its financial year gain as progress in US trade negotiations boosted investor sentiment.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 60.7 points, or 0.7 per cent, to 8574.9 by 2.10pm AEST on Monday, with eight out of the 11 sectors gaining. Health and technology led the advance.

on Friday and Nvidia towards $US4 trillion ($6.1 trillion) in market capitalisation. US futures point to further gains on Monday, while oil and gold are lower amid the increased risk-on environment.

Progress

Investors took profits from the big iron ore producers on the last day of the financial year, with Rio Tinto, Fortescue, and BHP all falling around 1.5 per cent.

Stocks in focus

In corporate news, James Hardie rose 6.2 per cent after shareholders in US outdoor decking company Azek approved a $14 billion buyout, which will see James Hardie shift its primary listing to New York.

Biotech company Tetratherix jumped 13 per cent in the first few minutes of its debut on the Australian sharemarket, in what is the latest of a handful of initial public offerings this month. It was trading around $2.96 by lunchtime.

DroneShield fell 5.5 per cent after earlier rallying on news it had won a $9.7 million Latin American defence contract. That’s after last week’s 33 per cent rally from announcing a major European deal.

NIB jumped 8.9 per cent after UBS upgraded the private health insurer to “buy” from “neutral” and set a short-term share price target of $7.85, which implies an upside of more than 20 per cent.

And Superloop jumped 2 per cent after the broadband provider said it expected underlying earnings to reach $91 million for the full year, beating its earlier guidance of $83 million to $88 million.

With Bloomberg

Canada drops digital tax to restart trade talks

Canada has withdrawn its digital services tax on technology companies such as Meta Platforms and Alphabet in a move to restart trade talks with the US.

“Rescinding the DST will allow the negotiations to make vital progress and reinforce our work to create jobs and build prosperity for all Canadians,” Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said in a social media post late Sunday (Monday AEST).

On Friday afternoon, US President Donald Trump said he was ending all trade discussions with Canada, one of its largest trading partners, in retaliation for the digital tax. He also threatened to impose a fresh tariff rate within a week.

Instead, Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney agreed the countries will restart negotiations and try to agree on a deal by July 21, according to a statement.

China factory activity decline eases again after trade truce

China’s factory activity improved for a second month but remained in contraction, as trade rebounded after the ceasefire in the tariff war with the US, while weak domestic demand weighs on the economy.

The official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index was 49.7 in June, versus 49.5 in the previous month, slightly exceeding the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of analysts. A reading below 50 indicates contraction. The non-manufacturing measure of activity in construction and services rose to 50.5 from 50.3 last month, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday. That compares with a forecast of 50.3.

The offshore yuan extended its gain after the data release and was 0.2 per cent stronger at 7.1626 per US dollar. Futures on 30-year US government bonds fell as much as 0.6 per cent – the most in a month – as traders dial back bets on further monetary easing.

For manufacturing, the new orders index expanded for the first time in three months, though a gauge of employment worsened again after a slight improvement in May. Among the 21 industries surveyed, more than half were in expansion territory, according to the statistics service. “Manufacturing production activities accelerated, and market demand improved,” Zhao Qinghe, a senior NBS statistician, said in a statement.

ASX climbs on trade talk hopes; James Hardie jumps

The Australian sharemarket was higher by lunchtime, tracking gains on Wall Street as progress in US trade negotiations boosted investor sentiment.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 23.6 points, or 0.3 per cent, to 8537.8 as of 12.05pm AEST on Monday, with eight out of the 11 sectors gaining, to finish the June quarter up by 8.91 per cent, making for the biggest June quarter since 2009. Health stocks and tech firms led Monday’s advance.

on Friday and Nvidia towards $US4 trillion ($6.1 trillion) in market capitalisation while gains in US futures pointed to further gains on Monday. Oil and gold both fell on Monday amid a more risk-on environment.

Progress

US President Donald Trump told the media over the weekend that said he did not think he needed to extend the July 9 tariff deadline for countries negotiating with the US.

Among the countries in talks, India is reported to have extended its stay in Washington to iron out a deal, Canada has withdrawn its digital services tax on technology companies to restart negotiations, and Taiwan has said it made “constructive progress”.

Stocks in focus

In corporate news, James Hardie rose 7.2 per cent after shareholders in US outdoor decking company Azek approved a $14 billion buyout, which will see James Hardie shift its primary listing to New York.

Biotech company Tetratherix jumped 13 per cent in the first few minutes of its debut on the Australian sharemarket, in what is the latest in a handful of initial public offerings this month. It was trading around $2.96 by Midday.

DroneShield fell 3.4 per cent after earlier rallying on news it had won a $9.7 million Latin American defence contract. That’s after last week’s 33 per cent rally after announcing a major European deal.

NIB jumped 5.8 per cent after UBS upgraded the private health insurer to “buy” from “neutral” and set short-term share price target of $7.85, which implies an upside of more than 20 per cent.

And Superloop jumped 2.4 per cent after the broadband provider said it expected underlying earnings to reach $91 million for the full year, beating its earlier guidance of $83 million to $88 million.

Chinese fund beats 97pc of peers

A 30-year-old Chinese fund manager is trouncing peers this year with a portfolio stocked with Gen Z-favoured names such as Pop Mart, betting that new-age shopping trends can help his fund overcome the country’s economic sluggishness.

Xie Tianyuan’s Penghua selected return flexible allocation mixed fund has returned 24 per cent this year, ranking in the top 3 per cent among roughly 2,300 peers, data from fund tracker East Money Information showed. That’s a turnaround from its recent past, when holdings in traditional sectors such as alcoholic beverages and farming dragged performance.

The Shenzhen-based fund manager, who took over early 2024, wasted little time in replacing what was then the fund’s top holding Kweichow Moutai, a baijiu distiller, with the maker of smash-hit Labubu dolls, Pop Mart. His repositioning for the fund, which has about $US7 million ($10.7 million) in assets under management, reflects how cultural shifts – brought on by digital influence and youth spending – are creating opportunities for Chinese investors navigating broader challenges in the world’s second-largest economy.

His conviction strengthened after witnessing the popularity of the toy maker’s products in Thailand, which, he says, signalled “non-linear growth with every metric showing breakout potential”.

Growing up immersed in Japanese anime culture – his desk is adorned with Dragon Ball Z figurines – Xie said he developed an eye for identifying promising characters or designs, called “IP brands”, by mixing personal fandom and online research. That he himself is demographically a member of Generation Z, the driving force behind China’s new “emotional spending” consumption trend, helps him understand what may resonate beyond advertising and go viral.

Gold extends decline as traders weigh trade talks

Gold edged lower after two consecutive weekly declines, with demand impeded by a risk-on mood as the White House aims to finalise trade deals with several nations ahead of a July 9 deadline.

Bullion fell as much as 0.8 per cent in early Asian trading before paring some losses. The European Union and the US believe they can clinch some form of trade agreement in time, Bloomberg reported on Friday (Saturday AEST), while talks with India, Japan and many others continue. Bloomberg has also reported that the US is nearing agreements with Mexico and Vietnam.

Still, if President Donald Trump’s only two other accords – with China and the UK – offer any indication, the pacts likely won’t be fulsome deals that resolve core issues and may leave many specifics to be negotiated later.

The precious metal remains up by about a quarter this year and is trading around $US230 short of a record high set in April, supported by demand for havens as investors grappled with elevated geopolitical and trade tensions. Still, gold is on track for its first monthly decline in 2025 as concerns about the Middle East conflict ease, and the US economy shows an improvement in consumer sentiment and inflation expectations.

Spot gold was down 0.2 per cent to $US3269.16 an ounce as of 8.24 am in Singapore (10.24am AEST). The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index slipped 0.1 per cent. Silver and palladium fell, while platinum rose.

Oil falls before OPEC+ supply decision

Oil fell following its biggest weekly loss in more than two years, as hedge funds piled into bearish bets after a fragile truce between Iran and Israel, and before a likely OPEC+ supply hike.

Brent dropped to near $US67 a barrel after sliding 12 per cent last week, while West Texas Intermediate traded around $US65. Iran said it remains sceptical that the US-brokered ceasefire with Israel will last, although President Donald Trump suggested he might back eventual sanctions relief for the Islamic Republic “if they can be peaceful”.

Key members of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies are ready to consider another 411,000 barrel-a-day increase for August when they meet on Sunday, according to several delegates. It would be the fourth month in a row that the group agreed on such a bumper hike, triple the initially planned volumes.

Oil is trading near where it started before Israel first attacked Iran on June 13, with the focus returning to supply and demand fundamentals. Apart from the potential OPEC+ increase, which may worsen a glut forecast for later this year, investors will be focused on trade talks, with just 10 days until Trump’s country-specific tariffs are set to resume.

item.title: Pimco’s Bowe wanted to be a stockpicker, but is picking bonds instead
item.description:
When Adam Bowe was studying music and psychology at university in Queensland, he would never have envisaged a 25-year career as a bond manager lay ahead, especially as he was more interested in the sharemarket.

But then, who does? Fixed income might be the world’s largest asset class but yield curves and basis points don’t quite have the same appeal as picking stock winners.

Bowe had even written to investment legend Warren Buffett as a youngster to ask him for a job, only to get a politely signed letter of rejection from the Oracle of Omaha.

“He said ‘we have the least people-intensive business on the planet, so we just don’t have room for anyone’,” Bowe recalled.

At the turn of the century Buffett came under pressure for avoiding tech stocks. When the tech boom turned to bust, he was vindicated, but it left an industry in tatters and jobs as equity analysts difficult to come by.

So while Bowe had managed to snare a summer job at equity fund Perennial Value under the guidance of Australian funds management legends Ian Macoun and John Murray, the prospect of a full-time equities role was grim.

Macoun, who later founded ASX-listed asset management firm Pinnacle, did, however, put in a good word for Bowe when he applied for a fixed-income analyst role at Queensland Investment Corporation. And so a life as a bond investor began.

Bowe eventually made his way to UBS Asset Management to work under Stuart Piper and later Anne Anderson, who fostered the career of many of today’s leading fixed-income managers.

He also spent two years at Paul Tudor-Jones’ hedge fund before the world’s top bond fund, Pimco, came knocking in 2011. “It wasn’t the perfect timing for me, but it was a perfect role for me,” Bowe says.

At the time, Pimco was overseen by the so-called bond king himself, Bill Gross. By 2014 Gross departed in a drama-filled palace coup. It was a tense period for the firm, that fought to convince clients not to pull their billions from the Newport Beach manager’s fund.

But the turbulence within Pimco was at odds with the distinct lack of excitement in the bond market. A decade of quantitative easing and zero, and even negative, interest rates made fixed income a tough sell.

“I had many nights where I sat there trying to figure out what other skill sets I had,” Bowe says of that time when bonds yielded nothing and prices barely moved.

A $40 billion opportunity

These days are a little different now that income and around-the-clock action has returned to the global fixed-income markets.

“If you look at this asset class relative to others, the starting point for expected returns are extremely attractive,” Bowe says.

Bowe has chaired Pimco’s Asian investment committee for the past seven years. But he is due to take charge of Pimco’s Australian portfolio management at the end of the year after long-standing head of the unit, Rob Mead announced his retirement.

Australia has always been a market where bonds have been relatively unpopular. Superannuation funds have the lowest allocation to fixed income in the developed world. Meanwhile, individuals have had their income needs met by high-yielding bank deposits, shares and hybrid securities that pay tax-beneficial franked distributions.

But increasingly Australian investors are buying more corporate and government bonds and Pimco’s local office, which oversees $65 billion, has been the fastest growing in the firm’s empire for the past two years.

This, according to Bowe, has been driven by demand from institutions for government bond and corporate debt exposure, with a reset higher in interest rates being an important factor.

Pimco and several other fixed income managers are eyeing the $40 billion of investments that are mainly tied up with individual investors in major bank hybrids as the prudential regulator phases out these securities.

“It was a hard asset class to compete with,” he says, given that the major banks have high credit ratings while the franked distributions were backed by the AAA-rated government.

While Pimco manages money for Australian clients, the $US2 trillion firm also invests in global bond markets on behalf of international investors.

For some time, it has held the view that Australian bonds are attractive because the market is underestimating the extent to which the Reserve Bank of Australia will have to cut interest rates.

(Typically when interest rates are lowered, the value of fixed rate bonds goes up as investors have locked in a more attractive interest rate.)

“We had a big difference of opinion versus the market and versus the RBA on how tight interest rates were,” Bowe adds.

“If you look at the percentage of household income that had to be dedicated to taxes and mortgage repayments, with a cash rate at 4.35 per cent it was as high as it has ever been.”

If not for public-sector spending and hiring, higher interest rate settings would have hurt the economy far more, Bowe says, which will constrain the RBA.

Where to for rates

“Given the levered nature of households, we do think interest rates will probably be lower here than places like the US,” he says.

The RBA has cut interest rates twice this year, to 3.85 per cent, and the tone of the governor Michele Bullock has turned decidedly dovish. The market currently expects the cash rate to fall to 3 per cent by the end of the year. Bowe believes the cash rate will fall by another 1 per cent from here.

“The risks are they have to go quicker and deeper,” he says.

For all the enthusiasm about bonds, the global market has been precarious for fixed-income traders. A sharp rise in long-term bond rates in the US, Japan and Europe reflects expectations of widening deficits that will be funded by more bonds that will have to be sold at higher rates.

Bowe says bring it on.

The bond manager says the sharp jump in long-term interest rates is creating opportunities for fixed-income funds to make attractive returns. And Australia looks like it won’t have any difficulties finding buyers. A recent Australian government bond tender received $84 billion of bids for a $15 billion raising.

The size of the government bond market has grown substantially in 25 years since Bowe began his career, while more local and international borrowers are tapping the market in bigger sizes and longer tenures.

It shows that Australian fixed income is well on the way to shedding its inferiority complex.

Bowe doesn’t seem to have any regrets of following a career path in fixed income, which he says requires a global view and working in a team to select securities and monitor the markets that influence them.

“You can be a great local equity manager with a highly concentrated portfolio that doesn’t really have to look at what’s happening around the world to be really successful,” he adds. “You can’t do that as a fixed-income portfolio manager.”

While Buffett’s message was that stock-picking isn’t labour-intensive, the same cannot be said about managing a bond portfolio across markets and maturities.

“If you like individual sports, we’re not for you. If you like team sports, we are.”

item.title: Regal’s former star trader now getting very unlikely help
item.description:
For a self-styled “private guy”, Deepan Pavendranathan has been catching people’s attention. In December last year, “Deeps” from Catalyst Funds Management hosted a Christmas party on a swanky boat on Sydney Harbour.

To liken it to a staff party might be underselling it. Catalyst doesn’t have many employees in Sydney. Instead, the bulk of the attendees were some of the city’s top brokers and investment bankers. Among them was Barrenjoey kahuna Matthew Grounds.

One reason that Sydney’s banker cohort will turn out for Deeps is because of the sheer amount of business he generates for them. He’s an unassuming whale in the market, known for his trading volume.

The Sri Lanka-born banker came up through Goldman Sachs, doing nine years at the global bank, becoming one of the best earners in the region.

In 2018, Regal’s Phil King poached him. He set up Regal’s successful Global Alpha fund. Unlike other fundies who may buy-and-sell based on conviction on a stock, Deeps’ speciality is looking for inefficiencies in the market. Buy lots of stock at a slim discount, then sell it before the market catches up. You can see why he’s such a popular bloke with bankers who clip tickets.

Deeps left Regal to form Catalyst in 2022. Not much can be learned about his performance at his own business. The fund’s website is a landing page with postal and email addresses.

Catalyst does, however, make disclosures to the US securities regulator.

The latest shows Deeps has $US382 million invested in the US stock market. It is spread across a staggering 448 different companies, with the largest a piddling $US13.1 million holding in Nvidia. The type of portfolio suggests Deeps moves in and out of positions regularly when he spots those inefficiencies.

Catalyst and Deeps have a smattering of local clients. But we hear one of the biggest backers is Schonfeld, the secretive hedge fund that operates the family office of maths genius Steven Schonfeld.

But what raised an eyebrow is Deeps and Catalyst seeking information from an unlikely source. Last month, Catalyst appeared on the national lobbyist register as a client for Premier National. It is best known for being the government relations shop run by Liberal party powerbroker Michael Photios, which also counts ex-Labor minister and Sky News panellist Graham Richardson as “senior counsel”.

The mere fact of a fund manager getting a lobbyist is exceedingly rare. Perpetual doesn’t have one. Neither does Magellan. Nor do Deeps’ old chums at Regal have need of them. The big asset managers like Blackrock and State Street don’t. Blackstone is on the books of GRACosway. But considering the amount of public-facing work around real estate that’s not really a surprise.

Why would Deeps need one? His type of investing really doesn’t lend itself to handshakes and public persuasion.

One possible rationale is that he’s looking for solid, actionable information wherever he can find it. Although, a political wheel-greaser like Photios seems like a very strange person to go to, doesn’t it? One former colleague of Deeps described him as a “very serious, smart quant guy”. Photios’ idea of alpha is getting a coffee meeting with a minister in the Liberal Party (which currently don’t exist), or say, the best Chinese knees-up in the CBD.

Strange timing, too, because Deeps was recently embroiled in a South Korean insider trading scandal that allegedly occurred during his time at Regal. Last year, this masthead identified Deeps as one of the people accused of breaching Korea’s short-seller laws around trading of semiconductor giant SK Hynix shares in 2019. Deeps and Regal rejected the allegations. Since then, the country has been thrown into a full-blown political crisis. This, perhaps, has given those involved in the scandal a reprieve.

Deeps declined to comment when asked why he had hired Premier National, or about his flashy boating sojourn at Christmas. He doesn’t court the media like so many of his other peers. We can respect that.

Still, coincidentally, a few hours after getting off the phone to us, Deeps posted on LinkedIn about his “Harbour event” from six months ago. He wrote Catalyst had raised “over $100k” for a Sri Lankan education charity called Palmera.

Even those who revel in the limelight know: what’s the point of raising money for charity if you don’t tell everyone about it?

item.title: ASX eyes the best return since COVID-19 as momentum trade kicks in
item.description:
The Australian sharemarket has recorded its biggest return for the financial year since the COVID-19 pandemic, defying expectations for a sustained sell-off in a period marked by uncertainty over the Trump administration’s tariff and economic plans and months of instability in the Middle East.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index has climbed 9.7 per cent for the 12 months through June and is expected to extend it gains by at least 0.1 per cent on Monday after a strong session on Wall Street that pushed the S&P 500 to a fresh record of 6170 and Nvidia towards the $US4 trillion ($6.1 trillion) mark.

A 10 per cent rally for the ASX 200 has only been surpassed by the 12 months to the end of June 2021, when equities rocketed more than 20 per cent as investors piled back into the market from the pandemic slump.

It’s been a remarkable turnaround for equities, not just in Australia but around the world, given it was just three months ago when US President Donald Trump rocked markets with his sweeping “liberation day” tariffs before agreeing to a 90-day pause that is set to expire in less than two weeks.

And it was only last week when oil spiked above $US80 a barrel after Trump authorised the bombing of Iranian nuclear sites, escalating the weeks-long war between Israel and Iran that raised the spectre of all-out war in the Middle East. And yet equities have continued to grind higher.

“I’m surprised that the headwinds for risk markets haven’t had a more substantial impact as yet,” said Stephen Miller, an investment strategy advisor to GSFM. “I would say markets are carelessly optimistic. Momentum won’t exist in perpetuity; there’ll be a catalyst that reverses things.”

In Australia, much of this year’s rebound has been driven by the financial sector, which has jumped 24 per cent, or more specifically by the blistering rally in the Commonwealth Bank, whose shares have rocketed 46 per cent and now account for more than 12 per cent of the benchmark.

Gold stocks have also benefited as central banks have bought up the precious metal and as investors seek out gold’s safe haven status amid the trade uncertainties and conflict between Israel and its neighbours.

Fund managers point out that foreign money has also continued to flow onto the ASX, especially into domestic names like Commonwealth Bank, as global investors look to diversify their exposure away from the United States.

Outside of banks and gold stocks, the ASX’s technology sector has jumped 24 per cent and discretionary retailers have also been well bid amid expectations of further rate cuts from the Reserve Bank of Australia.

‘Clear as mud’

Furniture retailer Temple & Webster is among the best-performing ASX 200 stocks this financial year, up 124 per cent, while electronics shop JB Hi-Fi has jumped 77 per cent. Property has also advanced, sending stocks like Charter Hall up 71 per cent.

VanEck managing director Arian Neiron said while momentum trading had pushed the sharemarket higher, markets would remain largely range-bound for the foreseeable future, with the odd spike in volatility.

“The narrative right now, I would argue, is it is as clear as mud,” he said. “You couldn’t confidently say with any real conviction where asset prices are going in the next three to six months.”

Except for the RBA’s board meeting next week, investors await any development in US trade negotiations, which remain in flux. As Trump touted progress on trade deals with a few countries and named agreements with China and the UK, he also spooked the market on Friday by ending talks with Canada in retaliation over a digital tax.

The 90-day pause on the US tariffs is set to expire around July 10, though Trump said that he may not stick to that timetable. Especially as his sweeping tax-cut and spending bill cleared a key procedural hurdle in the US Senate late Saturday night.

“Our view is that Trump’s not going to jack up tariffs again,” said Neiron. “Just because he’s got to get his ‘big beautiful bill’ ratified, so they won’t want to have too many external shocks to the market while they do that.”

Kris Bernie, a portfolio manager at bond fund manager Kapstream Capital, agreed that the next biggest catalyst for financial markets would be the bill.

“There’s still quite a bit of optimism about how the US administration will support the US economy, including the tax cuts,” he said. “If they come to fruition, it could provide a big boost to the US economy and offset any negatives from the imposition of higher tariffs.”
